A non-airbreathing engine carries both the fuel and the oxidizer required for combustion.
Rocket engines are the primary example of non-airbreathing engines.

The core of any gas turbine engine is the gas generator.
The gas generator consists of a compressor, a combustor, and a turbine.
The gas generator consists of a compressor, a combustor, and a turbine.
The gas generator consists of a compressor, a combustor, and a turbine.
The turbine extracts energy from the hot gas to drive the compressor.
A turbojet engine is formed by adding an inlet and an exhaust nozzle to the gas generator.
A turbojet engine is formed by adding an inlet and an exhaust nozzle to the gas generator.
A turbofan engine adds a fan driven by an additional turbine stage or a separate spool.
A turboprop engine uses a gas turbine core to drive a propeller through a reduction gearbox.
A turboshaft engine delivers power to a shaft to drive something other than a propeller, such as a helicopter rotor.
The ramjet engine has no moving parts (no compressor or turbine) and relies on forward speed to compress air.
A pulsejet engine operates with periodic or intermittent combustion using valves or acoustic geometry.
The uninstalled thrust (F_n) is the force produced by the engine alone, neglecting installation effects.
The installed thrust F is equal to the uninstalled thrust F_n minus the inlet drag D_inlet and the nozzle drag D_nozzle.
F = F_n - D_inlet - D_nozzle
F = F_n - D_inlet - D_nozzle
Drag associated with the engine intake aerodynamic forces.
Drag associated with the exhaust aft-end geometry and flow field.
Thrust specific fuel consumption (TSFC or S) is defined as the mass flow rate of fuel divided by the thrust.
Lower TSFC indicates a more fuel-efficient engine for a given thrust requirement.
Thermal efficiency is the ratio of the rate of kinetic energy production to the thermal power input from fuel.
Propulsive efficiency measures how effectively the engine's kinetic energy output is converted into aircraft propulsive power.
The overall efficiency of a propulsion system is the product of its thermal and propulsive efficiencies.
Specific thrust is the thrust produced per unit mass flow rate of air entering the engine.
The bypass ratio (alpha) is the ratio of the mass flow rate bypassing the core to the mass flow rate passing through the core.
High bypass ratio engines generally provide lower TSFC at subsonic cruise speeds.
The continuity equation expresses the principle of conservation of mass for a control volume.
The momentum equation expresses Newton's second law of motion for a fluid passing through a control volume.
The energy equation is a statement of the first law of thermodynamics applied to a fluid flowing through a control volume.
A flow is defined as steady if its properties at any point within the control volume do not vary with time.
A flow is one-dimensional if the fluid properties are uniform across any cross section perpendicular to the flow direction.
A perfect gas is a gas whose intermolecular forces are negligible and obeys the thermal equation of state P = rho*R*T.
A calorically perfect gas is a perfect gas with constant specific heats (c_p and c_v are constants).
The speed of sound 'a' in a calorically perfect gas is given by a = sqrt(gamma * R * T).
The Mach number M is defined as the ratio of the local fluid velocity V to the local speed of sound 'a'.
Flow where the local Mach number is strictly less than 1.0.
Flow where the local Mach number is strictly greater than 1.0.
Flow where the local Mach number is exactly equal to 1.0.
Stagnation temperature (or total temperature) T_t represents the temperature achieved when a fluid is decelerated to zero velocity adiabatically.
The increase in temperature associated with deceleration of a high-speed flow is called aerodynamic heating.
Stagnation pressure (or total pressure) P_t is the pressure attained when a fluid is brought to rest isentropically.
An isentropic flow is both adiabatic and reversible; entropy remains constant along a streamline.
The area-Mach number relation links the cross-sectional area of a duct to the local Mach number for an isentropic flow.
In a convergent duct, a supersonic flow slows down (Mach number decreases).
In a convergent duct, a subsonic flow speeds up (Mach number increases).
In a divergent duct, a supersonic flow accelerates (Mach number increases).
In a divergent duct, a subsonic flow decelerates (Mach number decreases).
The location of minimum cross-sectional area is called the throat, where the Mach number can reach unity.
When the Mach number at the throat reaches unity, the mass flow rate through the nozzle reaches its maximum possible value and is said to be choked.
A normal shock wave is a thin discontinuity perpendicular to the flow direction that can occur only in supersonic flow.
The Mach number always drops from a supersonic value upstream to a subsonic value downstream of a normal shock.
Static pressure increases significantly across a normal shock wave.
Static temperature increases across a normal shock wave.
The total pressure decreases across a normal shock, which represents an irreversibility (entropy rise) in the flow.
Because a shock wave is adiabatic, the stagnation temperature remains constant across it.
Fanno flow refers to adiabatic flow in a constant-area duct with friction.
Friction always drives the Mach number toward unity in Fanno flow, whether the inlet flow is subsonic or supersonic.
Rayleigh flow refers to frictionless flow in a constant-area duct with heat transfer (heating or cooling).
Maximum heat addition in a Rayleigh flow occurs when the Mach number reaches unity; further heating causes thermal choking.
Adding heat to a constant-area flow always results in a decrease in total pressure.
A rocket engine carries both its fuel and its oxidizer, allowing it to operate in a vacuum outside the atmosphere.
The total thrust of a rocket is the sum of the momentum thrust and the pressure thrust: F = m_dot * V_e + (P_e - P_a) * A_e.
The component of thrust generated by the change in momentum of the exhaust gas (m_dot * V_e).
The component of thrust due to the difference between exit pressure and ambient pressure ((P_e - P_a) * A_e).
The effective exhaust velocity C is defined such that F = m_dot * C, which combines momentum and pressure effects.
Specific impulse I_sp is the thrust divided by the propellant weight flow rate at sea level: I_sp = F / (m_dot * g_0).
The characteristic velocity c* is a measure of the combustion chemical energy and efficiency, independent of nozzle characteristics.
c* = (P_c * A_t) / m_dot. It depends primarily on combustion temperature and molecular weight.
The thrust coefficient C_f measures the amplification of thrust achieved by expanding the gas through the nozzle.
C_f = F / (P_c * A_t). It is a function of the pressure ratio and area ratio of the nozzle.
Maximum thrust for a given propellant mass flow and chamber condition occurs when the nozzle exit pressure equals the ambient pressure (P_e = P_a).
A nozzle is overexpanded if the exit pressure is lower than the surrounding ambient atmospheric pressure.
When a nozzle is highly overexpanded, oblique shocks or flow separation occur at the nozzle exit.
A nozzle is underexpanded if the gas exits at a pressure higher than the ambient atmospheric pressure.
Further expansion takes place outside the nozzle exit through expansion fans when P_e > P_a.
Liquid rocket systems utilize liquid chemical propellants stored in separate tanks.
High-thrust liquid rockets use turbopumps driven by a gas generator to force propellants into the high-pressure chamber.
A simpler feed system that uses regulated high-pressure gas to push propellants into the combustion chamber.
A solid rocket motor stores its fuel and oxidizer intimately mixed together as a solid block called the grain.
Combustion takes place on the internal surfaces of the hollow cavity inside the solid grain.
A grain geometry that causes the burning surface area (and therefore thrust) to increase over time.
A grain geometry that causes the burning surface area (and therefore thrust) to decrease over time.
A grain geometry where the burning surface area remains relatively constant during the burn.
The ideal rocket equation (Tsiolkovsky equation) is Delta_V = C * ln(m_i / m_f), neglecting gravity and drag.
m_i = m_PL + m_s + m_p.
The structural coefficient (epsilon) is the ratio of the structural mass to the sum of the structural and propellant masses.
Multistage rockets discard the dead weight of empty tanks and structures of depleted stages to achieve higher final velocities.
The ratio of the carried payload mass to the initial total mass of that specific rocket stage.
The objective of parametric cycle analysis is to relate the engine performance parameters to the design choices and the flight environment.
The gas turbine industry utilizes standard station numbering (e.g., 0 for ambient, 2 for compressor inlet, 3 for compressor exit, 4 for turbine inlet, 5 for turbine exit, 9 for nozzle exit).
Ideal cycle analysis assumes that the compression and expansion processes are reversible and adiabatic (isentropic).
It is assumed that combustion occurs at constant total pressure (no pressure drop in the combustor).
The working fluid is assumed to be a calorically perfect gas with constant specific heats throughout the engine.
The mass flow rate of fuel is neglected relative to the air mass flow rate in ideal performance matching (m_dot_f << m_dot_a).
The dimensionless parameter tau represents the ratio of stagnation temperatures across a component.
The dimensionless parameter pi represents the ratio of stagnation pressures across a component.
For ideal isentropic components (compressor or turbine), the total pressure ratio and total temperature ratio are directly coupled.
For a given maximum turbine inlet temperature, the specific thrust of an ideal turbojet drops to zero at a specific upper flight Mach number limit.
For a fixed flight condition and turbine inlet temperature, there is an optimum compressor pressure ratio that maximizes the specific thrust of a turbojet.
An afterburner increases the total temperature of the gas entering the exhaust nozzle without affecting the turbomachinery core.
The afterburner significantly increases the specific thrust by raising the exhaust velocity.
Afterburner operation causes a dramatic increase in TSFC due to fuel addition at lower pressure levels.
A turbofan engine divides the incoming air into a primary core stream and a secondary bypass stream.
alpha = m_dot_bypass / m_dot_core.
In a turbofan, a low-pressure turbine extracts energy from the core flow to drive the fan.
At subsonic cruise speeds, an ideal turbofan offers a significantly lower TSFC than a turbojet because of its higher propulsive efficiency.
There exists an mathematically optimum bypass ratio for a given core design that yields the absolute minimum TSFC.
A ramjet engine has no compressor or turbine; compression is achieved entirely through the dynamic pressure rise in the inlet.
An ideal ramjet cannot produce any thrust at zero flight velocity (Mach = 0) because it lacks a mechanical compressor.
For an unmixed ideal turbofan, the optimum kinetic energy distribution occurs when the exit velocity of the bypass nozzle equals the exit velocity of the core nozzle.
The performance of real components is characterized by total temperature ratios, total pressure ratios, efficiencies, and pressure losses.
The performance of the inlet (or diffuser) is primarily characterized by its total pressure ratio, pi_d = P_t2 / P_t0, also called the inlet recovery factor.
Military specifications (like MIL-E-5007D) define standard inlet recovery curves that decrease as the flight Mach number increases above 1.0.
The ratio of the actual mass flow entered into the inlet to the maximum possible mass flow that the capture area can intercept.
The isentropic compressor efficiency eta_c is defined as the ratio of ideal (isentropic) work to the actual work required for a given total pressure ratio.
tau_c = 1 + (pi_c^((gamma-1)/gamma) - 1) / eta_c, which links actual temperature rise to pressure ratio.
Polytropic efficiency (e_c for compressor, e_t for turbine) is defined as the isentropic efficiency of an elemental or infinitesimal stage.
For a constant polytropic efficiency e_c, the overall isentropic compressor efficiency eta_c drops as the total pressure ratio pi_c increases due to the preheating effect.
The isentropic turbine efficiency eta_t is defined as the ratio of actual work output to the ideal (isentropic) work output for a given total pressure ratio.
tau_t = 1 - eta_t * (1 - pi_t^((gamma-1)/gamma)), which relates the temperature drop to the expansion pressure ratio.
For a constant polytropic efficiency e_t, the overall isentropic turbine efficiency eta_t rises as the pressure ratio increases due to the reheating effect.
Combustion efficiency eta_b is the ratio of the actual thermal energy released to the chemical energy available in the fuel.
The total pressure ratio of the combustor pi_b = P_t4 / P_t3 is always less than 1.0 due to viscous friction and cold-to-hot flow momentum pressure drop.
Total pressure drops because of skin friction in the liner liners/swirlers and the fundamental thermodynamic loss from adding heat at finite Mach numbers.
The efficiency eta_AB measures how completely the fuel burns in the afterburner duct upstream of the exit nozzle.
The total pressure ratio pi_AB = P_t7 / P_t6 account for losses due to flameholders, friction, and high-temperature heat addition.
Mechanical efficiency eta_m accounts for frictional power losses in bearings and accessory gearboxes connecting the turbine and compressor shafts.
The exhaust nozzle performance is characterized by its total pressure ratio pi_n = P_t9 / P_t7, which represents friction losses in the nozzle duct.
An angularity factor (or divergence factor C_ang) accounts for the non-axial exit velocity vector at the nozzle plane, reducing net thrust.
Extraction of mechanical shaft power (P_TO) to run aircraft accessories directly reduces the turbine power available to drive the compressor.
Extracting high-pressure compressed air from the compressor exit for cabin environmental control systems (ECS) or turbine blade cooling reduces the downstream mass flow.
Reintroducing relatively cool bleed air into the turbine stages for blade cooling causes aerodynamic mixing losses and lowers the effective total temperature of the gas.
Analysis of real rocket engines requires accounting for non-ideal effects including nozzle efficiency, incomplete combustion, heat transfer, and complex chemical behaviors.
Due to high-velocity combustion and friction inside the chamber, the total pressure drops from the injector head to the nozzle throat entrance.
Nozzle efficiency eta_n is defined as the ratio of actual kinetic energy change to the ideal isentropic kinetic energy change across the nozzle.
The velocity coefficient C_v relates the actual exhaust velocity to the ideal velocity; typically C_v equals the square root of nozzle efficiency.
The discharge coefficient C_d is the ratio of actual mass flow rate to the ideal isentropic mass flow rate, accounting for boundary layer displacement.
Failure to achieve perfect chemical equilibrium or full mixing of oxidizer and fuel lowers the combustion temperature T_c below its theoretical adiabatic value.
Combustion efficiency is often expressed as the ratio of actual characteristic velocity (c*_actual) to the theoretical characteristic velocity (c*_theoretical).
Frozen flow assumes that the chemical composition of the exhaust gas remains constant (fixed at chamber exit state) during expansion through the nozzle.
Equilibrium flow assumes that chemical reactions occur instantaneously as pressure and temperature drop, continually adjusting composition to maintain local equilibrium.
Equilibrium flow gives higher calculated exhaust velocity and specific impulse than frozen flow because chemical recombination energy is recovered as kinetic energy.
The actual expansion process in a real rocket nozzle falls between the ideal frozen and shifting equilibrium bounds.
Heat loss through the chamber walls and nozzle liners directly reduces the thermal energy available for conversion into kinetic energy.
Regenerative cooling pumps the fuel or oxidizer through passages surrounding the thrust chamber wall to absorb heat before injection.
The heat absorbed by the coolant is reintroduced into the combustion chamber, preventing a net thermodynamic energy loss.
Injecting a small portion of fuel or inert gas along the internal wall creates a protective film that shields the structure from high-temperature core gases.
Liquid rocket engine cycles are classified into pressure-fed systems or pump-fed systems based on how propellants are pressurized.
A pump-fed open cycle where a fraction of the propellant is burned in a separate combustor to drive the turbine and is then exhausted overboard.
A high-pressure closed cycle where all pre-burner or gas-generator exhaust gases are directed into the main combustion chamber.
A closed cycle where fuel is vaporized in the cooling jacket and then routes directly through the turbine to drive the pumps before entering the injector.
The gas generator must operate off-stoichiometric (extremely fuel-rich or oxidizer-rich) to prevent melting the turbine blades.
Because the turbine exhaust is injected into the main chamber rather than dumped at low pressure, it allows extremely high chamber pressures (P_c) and higher efficiency.
In steady-state pump-fed cycles, the power produced by the turbine must equal the total mechanical power required to drive the oxidizer and fuel pumps.
The required shaft power for a propellant pump is proportional to the mass flow rate and pressure rise, divided by the pump efficiency (eta_p).
Real engine cycle analysis incorporates component efficiencies, pressure losses, mechanical losses, and bleeding to predict realistic performance.
In real engines, component total pressure ratios (like pi_d, pi_b, pi_n) are less than 1.0 due to friction and shock waves.
The net thrust of a real turbojet must account for exit velocity variations caused by nozzle efficiency (eta_n) and incomplete expansion.
Irreversibilities in the compressor and turbine increase entropy, directly decreasing the specific thrust and increasing the TSFC.
In a real turbojet, the turbine temperature drop is determined by the actual power required to drive the compressor: tau_t = 1 - (tau_lambda / tau_r) * (tau_c - 1) / (eta_m * (1 + f)).
The actual fuel-air ratio f accounts for combustor efficiency eta_b and variable specific heats across the burner.
The afterburner burns remaining oxygen in the turbine exhaust gas, but its efficiency (eta_AB) is lower than the main combustor.
Adding heat at a finite Mach number inside the afterburner duct causes a fundamental thermal total pressure drop (Rayleigh effect).
Real turbofan cycle analysis must track the independent losses and state changes in both the core and the fan bypass duct.
An engine configuration where the core and bypass streams exhaust through separate independent nozzles.
An engine configuration where the core and bypass streams mix in a common mixer component before expanding through a single nozzle.
For proper aerodynamic mixing, the core and bypass streams must enter the mixer at substantially equal static pressures (P_5 = P_15).
Aerodynamic mixing of streams with different total temperatures and velocities introduces viscous shearing losses, reducing overall total pressure.
Lower component efficiencies (like lower fan or turbine efficiency) shift the optimum bypass ratio (alpha) toward lower values compared to ideal cycles.
There is a distinct optimum fan pressure ratio (pi_f) that maximizes specific thrust or minimizes TSFC for a given bypass ratio and core technology.
A real turboprop splits the available turbine energy into shaft power to drive the propeller and a small amount of jet thrust from the exhaust.
The efficiency with which the propeller converts the brake shaft horsepower into effective aircraft propulsive power.
For turboprops, ESFC (or S_e) combines the propeller shaft power and residual jet thrust into a single performance parameter.
There is an optimum balance between how much expansion occurs in the turbine (for shaft power) versus the exhaust nozzle (for jet thrust) to maximize total equivalent thrust.
Extracting compressed air from the core compressor exit for aircraft usage causes an immediate penalty, reducing thrust and increasing TSFC.
Extracting mechanical power from the shaft forces the turbine to work harder, which reduces the total enthalpy available for the exhaust jet.
Engine performance analysis (or off-design analysis) predicts the performance of a specific engine across various flight conditions and throttle settings.
For a built engine, the physical throat areas of turbines and nozzles are geometrically fixed, which locks the aerodynamic coupling.
Corrected mass flow rate m_dot_c is defined as m_dot * sqrt(theta) / delta, allowing data from different conditions to be collapsed onto a single curve.
N_c = N / sqrt(theta). It relates the blade tip Mach number to the aerodynamic performance of turbomachinery.
Steady-state off-design operation requires that the mass flow entering a component matches downstream constraints, and the turbine power balances the compressor power.
If the high-pressure turbine nozzle guides are choked, the corrected mass flow exiting the compressor remains essentially constant, creating a fixed pumping constraint.
The steady-state compressor operating line on a compressor map is determined by the fixed throat area of the downstream turbine and exhaust nozzle.
When the convergent exhaust nozzle is choked, the operating pressure ratio across the turbine becomes independent of ambient pressure.
The fuel control unit (FCU) adjusts the fuel flow to match pilot thrust demands while keeping the engine within safety limits.
Mechanical stress restricts the maximum physical or corrected rotational speed of the fan spool.
Structural casing design restricts the maximum compressor exit pressure (P_t3) to prevent burst failure.
Material thermal properties restrict the maximum allowable gas temperature entering the turbine blades (T_t4).
Theta_break represents the ambient temperature point where the engine control transitions from limiting maximum compressor pressure ratio to limiting maximum turbine inlet temperature.
At low ambient temperatures (below theta_break), the engine is typically limited by mechanical limits like pressure or spool speed.
At high ambient temperatures (above theta_break), the engine control reduces fuel flow to protect the turbine from overheating, dropping the thrust.
A throttle hook is a curve showing the relationship between thrust and thrust specific fuel consumption at a constant flight condition as the throttle is varied.
During acceleration, the turbine power must exceed the compressor power to accelerate the spool rotor inertia, causing the operating line to transiently swing toward the stall line.
